hero.title: Find out which subscribers are in a botnet before your network ends up on a blocklist.
hero.lead: Horus Flow reads IPFIX flows from your MikroTik routers, recognizes every subscriber by IP and tells you which one is talking to command-and-control servers, scanning, joining a DDoS or sending spam, with the reasons and the RouterOS commands to act. It also watches the health of your routers and, if you turn it on, explains each finding with AI.
hero.note: Horus only reads and alerts: it never writes to your router.
hero.gridDesc: Illustration: each dot is a subscriber in 10.20.1.0/24. One of them, 10.20.1.47, is flagged as infected with 94% confidence.
hero.reason: Talks to a command-and-control server listed on Feodo Tracker
hero.news: New: AI assistant and router health

problem.title: One infected subscriber costs the whole ISP

blacklist.title: Blocklists
blacklist.body: When an IP on your network sends spam or attacks, reputation lists can block your addresses, and the trouble reaches subscribers who did nothing wrong.

abuse.title: Abuse reports without context
abuse.body: They arrive late, with an IP and a timestamp. Finding the subscriber, and knowing whether they are really compromised, is up to you.

link.title: Traffic nobody asked for
link.body: Outbound scans and attacks eat your uplink and fill your tickets before anyone in the NOC sees them coming.

problem.solutionTitle: Horus Flow tells you who, why and what to do

who.title: Who
who.body: Every IP seen in the flows is a subscriber, discovered automatically. Even behind the router's NAT, thanks to IPFIX post-NAT fields.

why.title: Why
why.body: Nine detectors and reputation lists such as abuse.ch and Spamhaus DROP. Every finding explains its reasons and its confidence.

what.title: What to do
what.body: RouterOS commands to isolate, rate-limit or notify, each with its undo command. You decide and apply them.

how.title: From the router to your NOC, without touching subscribers
how.lead: All you need is the main router of each node. Nothing to install on your subscribers' devices.
how.diagramTitle: How data flows through Horus Flow
how.diagramDesc: The MikroTik router exports IPFIX through a WireGuard tunnel to the Horus Flow server, which discovers subscribers, stores flows and detects botnets; results reach the NOC as dashboards, kiosk screens and alerts.

install.title: One-command install
install.body: On a clean Debian 12 or 13, one script installs everything and starts Horus on boot. horus-ctl upgrades with signed releases, takes a backup first and rolls back on its own if anything fails; PostgreSQL and ClickHouse are backed up every night. Works behind Nginx Proxy Manager.

motion.resilienceLabel: Animation: a storage component stops, flows wait in the buffer and drain when it comes back.
motion.resilienceCaption: ClickHouse, NATS or horus-app stopped for 30 s while ingesting 5,000 flows/s: 0 flows lost and the buffer drained in 12–20 s.

reliability.title: Reliability measured, not promised
reliability.lead: We tested the whole pipeline by killing components on purpose under constant traffic. These are the results and their conditions.

restart.test: Hard restarts (kill -9 and restart) of the collector, horus-app, NATS and ClickHouse, three times each, at 10,000 flows/s
restart.result: 0 flows lost, 0 duplicates and identical aggregates
restart.note: The only loss is what arrives over UDP while the collector is down; it is measured and shown.

clickhouse.test: ClickHouse down for 5 minutes at 20,000 flows/s
clickhouse.result: 0 loss; the backlog drains in about 2.5 minutes

platform.result: Alerts, findings, sessions, tunnels and kiosk come back on their own in 7–15 s

capacity.result: 10,000 flows/s meeting every criterion on 4 shared vCPUs

reliability.conditions: Test server: a virtual machine with 4 shared vCPUs and 16 GiB, running other workloads at the same time. The figures are a floor, not a ceiling.
reliability.projection: Projection for a 10,000-subscriber ISP: an 8 vCPU / 32 GB server and about 11 GB per day of raw flows (7 days of raw data; aggregates up to 25 months per subscriber and 5 years per node).

readonly.title: Never writes to the router
readonly.body: Its RouterOS user is read-only. You apply the recommended commands, if you want to.

isolation.title: Every ISP isolated
isolation.body: At every layer: row policies in PostgreSQL and ClickHouse, tenant-scoped events and ISP-scoped tokens.

access.title: Protected access
access.body: TOTP 2FA for administrators and rate limiting on the real client IP, also behind a proxy.

secrets.title: Encrypted credentials
secrets.body: Integration credentials are stored encrypted and are write-only.

pii.title: Less personal data
pii.body: Logs, the diagnostics bundle and the AI assistant only see masked subscriber IPs.

routers.a: MikroTik with RouterOS 7.12 or later. RouterOS 6 is not supported.

changes.q: Does Horus change anything on my router?
changes.a: No. You paste the onboarding script yourself: it creates the WireGuard tunnel, enables flow export and a read-only user. Horus never writes to the router, and the guide explains how to undo everything.

server.a: A clean Debian 12 or 13 (amd64). From 4 cores, 8 GB RAM and 100 GB SSD for about 300 subscribers, up to 8 cores, 32 GB and 500 GB NVMe for about 10,000.

domain.a: No. You can use just the server IP, a domain or subdomain with an automatic certificate, or put it behind your own proxy, such as Nginx Proxy Manager.

nat.q: Does it work with NAT on the router?
nat.a: Yes. With NAT on the main router, Horus uses IPFIX post-NAT fields to tell which subscriber each flow belongs to. It has been verified with a real MikroTik.

ipv6.a: Yes. IPv4 and IPv6 are treated as separate subscribers, and IPv6 is grouped by delegated prefix (/64 by default).

offline.q: Can it be installed without Internet access?
offline.a: Yes, with the offline installation package.

screenshots.q: Are the screenshots from real subscribers?
screenshots.a: No. Every screenshot on this page uses simulated data.

ai.q: What data does the AI assistant see?
ai.a: Only masked data: subscriber IPs are replaced with pseudonyms like “Subscriber 3 · 10.20.x.x”, and names, aliases and contact details are never sent. It ships turned off; each ISP decides whether to enable it.

localModel.q: Can I use AI without data leaving my network?
localModel.a: Yes. Besides Claude with your ISP's own key, you can point it at a local OpenAI-compatible server such as Ollama, vLLM or LM Studio. With a local model, no data leaves the ISP's network.

monitoring.q: How does it monitor my routers?
monitoring.a: It polls each MikroTik over SNMPv3 (CPU, memory, temperature, uptime and interfaces) and measures ICMP latency through the WireGuard tunnel. Every router gets one of eight states with its reason, using thresholds you can configure.

tv.q: Does it work on older TVs?
tv.a: Yes. Alongside the regular kiosk mode there's a lightweight ES5 build for smart TVs whose browser can't handle the full console.

detection.title: Signs of compromise, explained one by one
detection.body: Horus cross-checks reputation feeds against how each subscriber behaves. Every finding says what it saw, how confident it is and what you can do, with RouterOS commands you choose to apply.

points.c2: Contact with command-and-control (C2) servers from reputation feeds
points.scan: Outbound scanning and watched ports such as Telnet, TR-069 or SMB
points.spam: Direct outbound SMTP (spam) and DDoS participation
points.ddos: The DDoS rule no longer mistakes the TCP ACKs of a fast download for an attack
points.asn: Your own ASNs and custom reputation feeds per ISP
points.bulk: Resolve all findings of a type at once and mark false positives with a silence period

detection.alt: A critical finding: connections to a botnet control server listed on Feodo Tracker, with the evidence, the Analyze with AI panel and the suggested action of notifying the subscriber

customers.title: The IP is the subscriber, and their page tells the whole story
customers.body: Every IP seen in the flows is a subscriber, discovered automatically, even behind the router's NAT. Their page shows the status with its reasons, 24 h of traffic, what they use most and their findings, live.

mock.label: Animated illustration with simulated data: an AI analysis of a finding about contact with a botnet control server.
mock.title: AI analysis
mock.subject: Connections to a botnet control server (Feodo Tracker)
mock.p1: Subscriber 3 keeps completing connections to a command-and-control server listed on Feodo Tracker: 40 in the last 6 h, one every 60 s. That's the strongest sign of a compromised device.
mock.p2: Over the same window it sent direct SMTP to 86 different mail servers. The rest of its traffic looks normal for a residential subscriber.
mock.p3: Ask the subscriber to check their devices and, if they don't respond, block their outbound SMTP:
mock.cmd: /ip firewall filter add chain=forward src-address=$subscriber3Ip protocol=tcp dst-port=25 action=drop comment="Horus: SMTP"
mock.cmdNote: Horus never runs anything on your routers: copy the command if you decide to apply it.
mock.verifiedBody: Figures checked against Horus data · command from the verified catalog
mock.tools: Read-only tools: finding, subscriber flows, reputation

steps.title: How it works
steps.lead: Four steps, always in the same order. The assistant never acts on its own.

ask.title: You ask for an analysis
ask.body: “Analyze with AI” on a finding or on a router's page.

mask.title: Horus masks the data
mask.body: Subscriber IPs become pseudonyms like “Subscriber 3 · 10.20.x.x”. Names, aliases and contact details never leave.

tools.title: The AI queries read-only
tools.body: It uses read-only tools with the permissions of whoever asked: it sees what you can see, nothing more.

verify.title: Horus checks the answer
verify.body: It compares the answer against its own data and labels it Verified or Partially verified; anything unsupported is flagged.

privacy.title: What the AI sees, and what it doesn't
privacy.lead: Before anything is sent, Horus swaps each subscriber for a pseudonym. The answer comes back with the pseudonym, so you know who it is; the model doesn't.
privacy.maskLabel: Example with simulated data: IP 10.20.1.47 and its alias become the pseudonym Subscriber 3 · 10.20.x.x before reaching the model.

sees.behavior: Behavior: ports, destinations, volumes and patterns

verify.title: Answers that are checked, not made up

items.numbers: Every data point is checked against what Horus knows about your network
items.catalog: Suggested RouterOS commands come from a verified catalog
items.flagged: Data or commands that can't be checked are flagged
items.never: Horus never runs anything on your routers: you decide

routers.q: Can the AI change anything on my routers?
routers.a: No. It suggests RouterOS commands from a verified catalog, but Horus never runs anything on your routers: you apply them if you want to.

data.a: With a local model (Ollama, vLLM, LM Studio), no. With Claude, only masked data leaves: pseudonyms instead of subscriber IPs, and never names, aliases or contact details.

cost.a: With Claude, usage is billed to your ISP's own API key; with a local model there's no per-query cost. The daily limit helps keep spending in check.

default.a: No. It's off for every ISP until someone enables it and picks a provider.

history.a: Masked analyses are kept so you can reread them without spending queries, 90 days by default. The audit log records who asked, the provider, the model, tokens and tools.

monitoring.title: The health of every MikroTik, right next to your network's security
monitoring.lead: Horus polls your routers over SNMPv3 and measures their latency through the WireGuard tunnel. Eight states, each with a reason, tell you which one needs attention, without alerts that come and go.

grid.title: Router health

cpu.title: CPU
cpu.body: Processor load, with warning and critical thresholds.

memory.title: Memory
memory.body: How much of the router's memory is in use.

temperature.title: Temperature
temperature.body: Spot a device running hot before it reboots.

interfaces.title: Interfaces
interfaces.body: Status and traffic for every interface.

latency.title: Latency
latency.body: ICMP through the WireGuard tunnel, from the router to Horus.

states.title: Eight states, each with its reason
states.lead: A state never shows up alone: it always says why. Colors always come with their name.

online.label: Online
online.body: Responding, with every metric within thresholds.

warning.label: Warning
warning.body: A metric crossed the warning threshold, such as high CPU or temperature.

critical.label: Critical
critical.body: A metric crossed the critical threshold: time to act.

degraded.label: Degraded
degraded.body: Responding, but with high latency or packet loss.

stale.label: Stale
stale.body: The latest data is too old to rely on.

unknown.label: Unknown
unknown.body: Not enough data yet, for example right after it was added.

maintenance.label: Maintenance
maintenance.body: Marked for maintenance: no alerts while it lasts.

hysteresis.title: Hysteresis: no flapping alerts
hysteresis.body: A spike lasting a few seconds doesn't change the state. Horus waits for a condition to hold before switching and for it to clear before switching back, so your NOC doesn't chase alerts that fix themselves.
hysteresis.chartLabel: Illustrative chart: CPU crosses the threshold for a moment and the state doesn't change; once it stays above, the router goes to Warning, then back to Online when it recovers.

detail.title: A page for every router

detail.label: Illustration with simulated data of a router's page.

thresholds.body: Thresholds are configurable, so each state means the same in Horus as it does in your NOC. Wondering why a router is in Warning? Click “Analyze with AI” on its page.

noc.title: Your NOC on any TV, no keyboard or mouse required
noc.lead: Pair a screen with an 8-character code, pick a playlist and let it rotate dashboards on its own. If the network drops, it keeps showing the latest data and tells you since when.

tv.label: Illustration: a kiosk screen rotating between the ISP NOC and Security dashboards (simulated data).
tv.altNoc: Kiosk at 1920×1080 showing the ISP NOC dashboard: traffic, active subscribers, findings, exporters and top subscribers with masked IPs
tv.altSecurity: Kiosk at 1920×1080 showing the Security dashboard: open findings, botnet signals, watched ports, 7-day trend and recent findings

steps.title: From TV to video wall in three steps

enroll.title: Pair the screen
enroll.body: With a one-time 8-character code. Each screen is a read-only device, not a user.

playlist.title: Choose what rotates
playlist.body: Playlists with dashboards and how long each one shows. Changes reach the TVs without pairing them again.

forget.title: Forget about it
forget.body: It updates itself and recovers after an outage. While offline, it keeps the latest data with an “Offline since” notice.

dashboards.title: Three dashboards, ready to go
dashboards.lead: Use them as they are or build your own from the widget gallery.

noc.title: ISP NOC
noc.body: Current and 24 h traffic, active subscribers, exporters, top categories and subscribers, and recent findings.
noc.alt: ISP NOC wall at 1280×720 with traffic, active subscribers, findings, exporters, categories, subscribers and recent findings

security.title: Security
security.body: Findings by severity, botnet signals, watched ports, security by node and the 7-day trend.

routers.title: Router health
routers.body: Summary by state and the routers that need attention, to rotate alongside the others.

resolution.title: Readable from 1280×720 to 4K
resolution.body: Compact layouts that scale with the screen: the same on an HD TV as on a 4K video wall. The screenshots on this page are at 1280×720, the smallest size.

lite.title: A lightweight build for older TVs
lite.body: An ES5 kiosk with no modern dependencies, for smart TVs whose browser can't handle the full console. Same dashboards, lighter requirements.

privacy.title: Made for a room with visitors
privacy.body: The kiosk is read-only and can show subscriber IPs masked.
